                         STAFF’S STATEMENT IN OPPOSITION TO STIPULATION
         The Utility Division Staff (“Staff”) of the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission

(“Commission”, “NMPRC” or “PRC”), files Staff’s Statement in Opposition to Stipulation

(“Statement in Opposition”), to the Comprehensive Stipulation filed by Southwestern Public Service

Company (“SPS”), on June 22, 2026. Pursuant to the Hearing Examiner’s June 18, 2026, Order

Revising Procedural Deadlines, statements in opposition to any stipulation in this matter shall be filed

by June 29, 2026, thus Staff’s Statement in Opposition is timely filed. Staff would show the

Commission that the black box agreement to implement an increase in New Mexico retail base

rate revenues $90,000,000, effective December 1, 2026, is not in the public interest and is inconsistent

with Staff’s Direct Testimony of Ed Rilkoff and Peterson Brossy1. Further, the $90 million amount

is far from Staff’s recommended $47 million revenue deficiency and is a “black box”2 amount that

    leaves the public and the Commission in the dark about what exactly was decreased from the

                                                     original $172

                                           PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND3


       1.      On November 20, 2025, using a Future Test Year running from December 1, 2026,

through November 30, 2027, SPS filed its Application requesting authorization to revise its New

Mexico retail rates under Advice Notice 341 and other associated relief. SPS’s Application sought a

base rate revenue increase for the New Mexico retail jurisdiction of $175,354,544, a 24.25% increase

over current base rate revenue and 16.73% increase in total revenues, based on a total New Mexico

retail revenue requirement of $892,652,373.

       2.      SPS and a number of intervenors 4 (the “Stipulating Parties”), filed the Opposed

Stipulation (“Stipulation”), stipulating to the resolution of certain issues in the interests of the

signatories. Staff did not join the Stipulating Parties as the Opposed Stipulation did not address Staff’s

concerns and the public interest. The concise reasons are discussed in the following paragraphs.

           6.      The Commission’s Rules (the “Rules”), provide that the Commission “recognizes that

    parties to a proceeding and staff may reach compromises and settle some or all issues. Settlement

    stipulations shall be binding only if approved by the commission.” 1.2.2.20 NMAC.

           7.      In cases where stipulations are contested, as in the present matter before the

     Commission, the Rules further provide5,

                   (1)     If some, but not all, of the parties to a proceeding, including staff, enter
                   into a stipulation seeking to dispose of some or all of the issues in the
                   proceeding, the stipulation shall be filed and copies presented to the presiding
                   officer and served on the parties or staff opposing the stipulation. If the
                   proceeding is before the commission en banc, the commission may in its
                   discretion assign a hearing examiner to preside over any public hearing to be
                   conducted on the stipulation. When filed and presented, the stipulation must be
                   accompanied in rate cases by a reconciliation statement showing the dollar
                   impact of the settlement and the resulting rates. This statement shall contain the
                   information listed in Subsection F of 1.2.2.36 NMAC.
                   (2)     Parties or staff opposing the stipulation shall file statements briefly
                   setting forth the grounds upon which they oppose the stipulation in writing
                   within five (5) days after the stipulation is served, or orally at the public hearing,
                   whichever occurs first. Responses by staff or parties supporting the stipulation
                   shall be made as directed by the commission or presiding officer.



5
  (1)     The commission or presiding officer shall schedule the stipulation for public hearing and review unless it is determined
that the nature and extent of the opposition is such that hearing the stipulation will not materially conserve commission, staff, and
party resources. In the event this determination is made, the commission or presiding officer may refuse to entertain the stipulation.
The commission or presiding officer also has the discretion to combine a public hearing on a contested stipulation with the public
hearing on the merits of any substantive issues not addressed by the stipulation.
(2)       A public hearing shall be conducted to determine whether the stipulation shall be approved by the commission. The
proponents of the stipulation have the burden of supporting the stipulation with sufficient evidence and legal argument to allow the
commission to approve it. At the public hearing all parties and staff shall be allowed an opportunity to present evidence and cross-
examine opposing witnesses on the stipulation.
(3)       In cases heard by a hearing examiner rather than the commission the hearing examiner may:
(a)       decide that the settlement stipulation should not be certified to the commission at all, in which event the hearing examiner
may indicate to the parties and staff whether additional evidence or legal argument in support of the stipulation or amendments to
the stipulation might meet the hearing examiner’s reservations about the stipulation; or
(b)       certify the settlement stipulation to the commission for its review; the certification shall include a recommended
disposition of the stipulation, whether the recommendation be positive or negative or otherwise suggest a manner of disposition;
exceptions to the certification may be filed within ten (10) days after the date the settlement stipulation is certified to the
commission, unless the commission or presiding officer directs otherwise.

                                                     DISCUSSION

             Staff’s opposition to the Stipulation is based upon the public interest in fair, just, and

reasonable rates. The last two SPS rate cases have all been determined by uncontested stipulations.

Accordingly, it is in the public interest for the opposed issues to be vetted at a public hearing before a

hearing examiner so that a record can be developed upon which the Commission can make a final,

precedential determination, on those issues. For the reasons discussed below, and set out in detail in

Exhibit A, attached hereto, Staff opposes the Stipulation, as filed, on two main grounds:

    I.      Jurisdictional allocation and regulatory clarity: Staff’s opposition is premised on the need

    for certainty that only the Commission can provide through a ruling on the appropriate treatment of

    New Mexico-specific resources and costs within SPS’s multi-jurisdictional system. Absent Staff’s

    opposition, the Commission lack the opportunity to resolve these important methodological issues.6

    Staff witnesses Rilkoff, Blank, and Brossy each address this issue from complementary perspectives:

    Rilkoff identifies the affordability concerns confronting New Mexico retail customers in the multi-

    jurisdictional context; Dr. Blank addresses the jurisdictional allocation methodology that drives those

    affordability concerns; and Brossy quantifies the resulting overstatement of SPS's revenue

    requirement.

            The evidentiary basis for Staff's position rests principally on the testimony of Dr. Blank, who

    identifies a fundamental flaw in SPS's jurisdictional cost allocation. Specifically, SPS applies

    forecasted 12-CP and energy allocation ratios in New Mexico while Texas and FERC do not employ

    the same forecasted methodology. Dr. Blank argues that because SPS projects significantly higher

    load growth in New Mexico than in Texas, SPS’s use of a forecasted test period in New Mexico —


6
  Staff witness Dr. Larry Blank’s recommendations address the affordability concerns also discussed in Staff witness Ed Rilkoff’s
testimony.
     Page 3 of 7
     Docket No. 25-00079-UT
     Staff’s Statement in Opposition to Stipulation
     while Texas uses a historical base year, risks double recovery and an overstatement of the New

    Mexico revenue requirement. Therefore, to correct this asymmetry, Dr. Blank recommends that the

    Commission, for jurisdictional allocation purposes, require SPS to use a base-year/Texas-consistent

    methodology, with adjustments limited to known and measurable changes. Dr. Blank's methodology,

    standing alone, reduces the revenue deficiency by approximately $56.7M.

           When combined with Staff witness Brossy’s adjustments, Staff’s overall revenue deficiency

    is approximately $47 million-- a figure that is irreconciliable with the Stipulation’s revenue deficiency

    of $90 million. See, Table PB-2 (page 10). Critically, the issue is broader than the dollar amount. As

    Rilkoff's testimony makes clear, that $42M gap between Staff's adjusted figure and the Stipulation

    translates directly into rates that are neither just nor reasonable for New Mexico customers. That

    disparity compels Staff's opposition to the Stipulation, and Staff respectfully urges the Commission

    to reject the $90M figure and instead adopt a revenue requirement consistent with the evidentiary

    record and Brossy's Direct Testimony.

          The import of this issue is not confined to the current proceeding. In Case No. 25-00066-UT,

    the Commission’s final order approved approximately $9 billion of SPS resources to be added to its

    system and SPS will within the next 2 years, place those resources into base rates. In that case, the

    Commission established some ratemaking principles to avoid double charging of New Mexico

    customers and cross subsidization of Texas by New Mexico that should be followed in this case for

    consistency in jurisdictional allocation methodology as follows7:

              105. Based on the foregoing, the following ratemaking principles applicable to
              jurisdictional allocation are established:

          In this case, a Commission’s ruling on jurisdictional allocation methodology would therefore

 further establish the governing precedent in advance of SPS’s next rate case where the 25-00066-UT

 resources may be requested to be placed into rate base.

I.        Class allocation: Dr. Blank’s class revenue allocation and banding recommendations provide

a technical ratemaking approach for producing a more balanced distribution of the approved revenue

increase than SPS’s as-filed proposal. The stipulation still places disproportionate increases on

residential and smaller customer classes. Even though the stipulation reduces SPS’s overall requested

increase, Residential and Small General Service still receive 17.50% increases, while Primary General

Service and LGS-T classes receive increases of only about 10.4%. As Staff has testified, much of the

increase appears to be driven by system costs related to large-load customers. Therefore, residential

and small commercial customers should not bear rate increases that are greater than the average

increase.

II.        Other Provisions in the Stipulation: Because Staff opposes the stipulation on two major

issues, there are several additional provisions that are difficult to disaggregate that Staff cannot accept

at this time. Accordingly, Staff’s opposition to the stipulation, as a whole, continues to rest on its direct

testimony. However, to the extent provisions of the Stipulation are consistent with Staff’s filed
      Page 5 of 7
      Docket No. 25-00079-UT
      Staff’s Statement in Opposition to Stipulation
 positions, Staff does not oppose those provisions, and conversely, Staff opposes those provisions that

are inconsistent with Staff’s direct testimonies. for the same reasons as testified to which are

incorporated herein by reference. Staff’s specific positions on each provision are set forth in the

attached Exhibit A. Staff will not file new testimony with respect to the provisions it does not oppose

or on which it takes no position, and will instead rely on its pre-filed Direct Testimony for those

matters. On July 7, 2026, Staff will file testimony in Opposition to the provisions of the Stipulation it

opposes as set out in Exhibit A.

                                                     CONCLUSION

        The Commission approved SPS’s last two rate cases based upon uncontested stipulations,

deferring crucial issues pertaining to jurisdictional allocation between New Mexico and Texas

customers. Yet, as a policy matter, the Commission has also expressed concerns with black box

settlements that do not provide transparency to ratepayers and defer resolution of important matters

undetermined a future proceeding. Accordingly, Staff views its opposition to the Stipulation as

presenting the Commission the opportunity to address critical issues that have a direct bearing the

affordability of rates. Staff believes it is important to resolve these matters now—before resources

approved in 25-00066-UT are placed into rates in the next two years.

    Respectfully submitted this 29th day of June, 2026.

STAFF OPPOSES FROM THIS POINT ON. The valuation methodology shall calculate the
net ACAP benefit by adjusting the seasonal C1 BESS ACAP for the applicable seasonal planning
reserve margin ("PRM"), as follows:
       1.      Summer Period (May through October): The C1 BESS ACAP value assigned to
               New Mexico shall equal the summer C1 BESS ACAP divided by one plus the
               applicable summer PRM.
       2.      Winter Period (November through April): The C1 BESS ACAP value assigned to
               New Mexico shall equal the winter C1 BESS ACAP divided by one plus the
               applicable the winter PRM.
This methodology is specific to this proceeding and shall not be precedential. SPS shall initiate a
stakeholder process to evaluate the treatment of directly assigned resources and the jurisdictional
allocation of divergent state resource portfolios for future proceedings.

recover through its FPPCAC the capacity costs from the Battery Energy Storage System LTPPAs

       1.5.    SPS Short-Term Capacity Needs
STAFF DOES NOT OPPOSE: SPS withdraws without prejudice its request to recover SPP
deficiency payments through the FPPCAC. SPS will use its best efforts to address short-term

       B. Investment Tax Credits for Cunningham BESS and Plant X
BESS SPS is authorized to treat the investment tax credits (“ITCs”) for the Cunningham BESS
and Plant X BESS as follows:

       costs, capped at 10% of the corresponding ITCs’ nominal value, for future recovery.
       (d) SPS may apply a return at the stipulated WACC to the unamortized balance of the

 EXHIBIT A


STAFF TAKES NO POSITION: SPS agrees to collaborate with Walmart Inc. and other
interested stakeholders regarding the development of a new electric vehicle rate specifically
designed for public-facing Direct Current Fast Charging facilities. SPS shall initiate a stakeholder
process within sixty (60) days following the Commission’s final order in this proceeding and report
on that process in its next Transportation Electrification Plan filing. Based on those workshops,
SPS shall file a proposed DCFC-specific rate, tariff, or rate design with the Commission.
       1.20. Data Centers and Large Load Tariffs
STAFF DOES NOT OPPOSE: SPS shall develop and file for Commission approval a new Large
Load customer class and tariff within six (6) months following the Commission’s final order in
this proceeding and include the Large Load customer class in its cost-of-service study in its next
base rate case. The proposed class and tariff shall be designed to ensure that all costs attributable
to serving Large Load customers are assigned to that class and do not shift costs or risks to any
other customer class. SPS will gather intervenor input on the Large Load Tariff prior to filing.
